And when they saw their great numbers,
and that they themselves had no strength,
they turned back and entered the city.
And they crossed the Tigris,
and went and went up to the monastery of Mar Mattai,
and remained there a few days.
Now the accursed brigands, when they entered the city,
the Arabs, the inhabitants of the city, met them with abundant food and cold water.
And they rejoiced over them with great joy,
and were elated, thinking that it was only the Christians that they were going to plunder, take captive, and kill.
Now the Christians who were in the neighborhood of the Church of the Tagritans
took their wives, their sons, and their daughters, along with all their possessions,
and went and took refuge in the courtyard of the cousin of the Prophet,
the one who is called Naqib al-Alawiyyin {OCR?},
thinking that when the brigands showed honor to that courtyard,
they would be saved there from the slaughter and captivity of the city.
But the rest of the Christians,
who had no place to flee and take refuge in the courtyard of the Naqib,
remained in their houses, fearful and trembling, weeping and lamenting over themselves and their misfortune,
though in truth, the misfortune was for those who had gone there.
Now as soon as the brigands entered,
they began asking about the Christians.
And the Arabs, the inhabitants of the city, cried out with one voice:
"Behold, all the Christians are in the courtyard of the Naqib!"
Then they took courage,
and all of them went there.
And they set up ladders, mounted, and captured the courtyard,
and plundered and took captive all the people there.
And one of the Christians there was struck by an arrow and died.
And they maltreated not only the Christians, but also the Arabs:
they outraged their wives, sons, and daughters inside the mosques before their eyes.
And when they had finished,
they went also to the neighborhood of the Jews,
and plundered their houses,
and took captive all their people.
As for the Christians who had remained in their houses and had not gone anywhere,
no one harmed them,
nor did they even see the brigands with their eyes.
Yes, certain Christian merchants and many Arabs
who had come to the city
and were staying in the inns outside the city,
where none of the brigands reached,
